To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
scaling up aid in Tanzania will have positive impact on GDP growth and will not necessarily lead to a real exchange rate appreciation.

(i) the Dutch disease is not a serious concern in a scenario where aid-financed public investment increases productivity in the non-tradable sector; and (ii) aid-financed public spending can be used to increase the growth rate in a country with a high aid dependence, without causing a Dutch disease.
aid-financed public investments can contribute to economic growth in Tanzania, but only under the condition that the aid is used to increase public capital and not to increase public consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of scaling up aid on the economy of Tanzania and in particular on the risk of a Dutch Disease.
the question whether aid can be used to reduce the Dutch disease risk.
the impact of scaling up aid in a country with a high degree of aid dependence and a high degree of openness to trade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Dutch disease effect is not an issue in Tanzania.
aid can be an effective instrument for development in Tanzania, but that the effectiveness of aid is highly dependent on how aid is spent and the quality of economic policies in place.
aid can help Tanzania to achieve a higher and sustained economic growth rate but only if it is used in an efficient way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aid-financed public investment in Tanzania is a good thing as long as the economy has the potential to increase its productivity.
aid-financed public investments in Tanzania would not necessarily result in the Dutch disease.
aid can have a positive impact if it is used in a prudent way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Dutch Disease does not have to be a problem in a country that is able to increase productivity.
aid-financed public spending has a potential to increase productivity in the long run and thus reduce the risk of the Dutch Disease.
the Dutch disease does not have to occur in a country with a high degree of aid dependence if productivity effects are positive.
